result.summary: Two decisions, both answerable now. (B) The comparison value should be a single scalar type, not a union: the vendors' own strict-mode reference example for exactly querbeet's column/operator/value shape types `value` as `anyOf[string, number, object]`, and no vendor documents any rule for which branch a model picks — that permissive union IS the schema shape that produced the measured 4-to-1 split. The only documented mechanism that removes the ambiguity is grammar-constrained sampling against one declared type (Anthropic's worked case: unconstrained `"two"`/`"2"` becomes always `2`), and querbeet cannot invoke it because Recipes arrive by copy-paste. Recommendation: `value` is a JSON number in canonical machine form for numeric columns, with querbeet coercing a canonical numeric string on ingest and refusing a locale-formatted one by name in the same validator that already checks column names; runner-up is the always-a-string-plus-column-locale form the plan currently leans to, which is weaker because it re-imports the `1.234` ambiguity R1/R3 already measured into the value field. The per-format survey largely did not survive verification: only JsonLogic's row is confirmed, and it is neither typed-by-syntax nor coerced nor type-bracketed — the spec documents no coercion rule at all for `>`/`>=`/`<`/`<=`, so behavior is whatever the host implementation does, and the failure mode is silent divergence rather than an error. (C) Yes, a utility framework can be inlined next to Vue Flow's stylesheet: Tailwind v4 documents dropping Preflight by splitting `@import "tailwindcss"` into its three layer imports and deleting only the `preflight.css` line, which leaves utilities plus theme and no reset to clobber `@vue-flow/core/dist/style.css`. Runner-up: hand-written scoped CSS. Pico.css is the weakest of the three because it is classless and restyles bare elements globally with no documented opt-out.

findings.claim: DECISION B — Union types (anyOf number|string) are the wrong answer, and are the direct explanation of the measured split. Microsoft's structured-outputs doc ships a `strict: true` function-calling example of exactly querbeet's shape (conditions[] of column/operator/value) whose `value` is `anyOf[{string},{number},{object column_name}]`, with no description, no discriminator and no per-column typing. Strict mode still admits both "1000" and 1000 for the same condition, so the choice is left entirely to the model.
sources: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/foundry/openai/how-to/structured-outputs (REST zone pivot, section "Function calling with structured outputs")
findings.evidence: Verbatim schema fragment confirmed at the primary source (ms.date 2026-05-13): "value": {"anyOf": [{"type":"string"},{"type":"number"},{"type":"object","properties":{"column_name":{"type":"string"}},"required":["column_name"],"additionalProperties":false}]}. The doc's own unsupported-keywords table forbids `pattern`/`format` on strings and `minimum`/`maximum` on numbers, so a schema author has fewer tools than plain JSON Schema to narrow the branches. Two wording nits from verification: the doc uses SQL glyphs (">") where querbeet uses names ("gt"), and the union is non-discriminated rather than untyped.

findings.claim: DECISION B — No vendor documents any determinism or consistency property for union branch selection. OpenAI's structured-outputs guide lists `anyOf` as supported but its only guarantees are schema adherence ("the model will always generate responses that adhere to your supplied JSON Schema") and key ordering. The union-with-null pattern is documented solely to emulate optional parameters; a two-primitive scalar union such as {"type":["number","string"]} appears nowhere on the page. Silence, not endorsement.
findings.evidence: Verified verbatim against raw HTML (1.7 MB, 12 `anyOf` occurrences, tag-stripped): "Root objects must not be anyOf and must be an object", "For anyOf, the nested schemas must each be a valid JSON Schema per this subset", and "it is possible to emulate an optional parameter by using a union type with null." Exhaustive grep for "determinis"/"consistent"/"always generate" found only the adherence and key-order guarantees; the single hit for "consistent" is a marketing bullet about formatting. Practical consequence for querbeet: a number|string `value` is not a supported-and-safe schema, it is an unspecified one.

findings.claim: DECISION B — A single declared scalar type is the only documented mechanism that actually removes the ambiguity, and it acts at the sampler rather than through prompt wording or examples. Anthropic's worked case is querbeet's failure mode verbatim: for `passengers: int`, unconstrained output may be "two" or "2"; with `strict: true` the response always contains 2. The same page independently names the exact defect the FR-28 spike measured — "Claude might return incompatible types (\"2\" instead of 2)".
findings.evidence: Verbatim: "Setting strict: true on a tool definition guarantees Claude's tool inputs match your JSON Schema by constraining the model's token sampling to schema-valid outputs (a technique called grammar-constrained sampling)." GA, not beta-gated ("generally available on the Claude API for Claude 4.5 and later models"; the old beta header is deprecated). A plain {"type":"integer"} uses none of the unsupported keywords. Load-bearing caveat carried from verification: strict tool use is an API-side feature and querbeet is an offline file:// app whose Recipe is pasted in from an arbitrary chat, so querbeet cannot invoke the mechanism — it can only imitate its effect by declaring one type in the prompt block and enforcing it on ingest. Note the direction of the vendor's framing: the number is the target, the string is the error.

findings.claim: DECISION B, format survey — JsonLogic: the value is NEITHER typed-by-syntax, NOR coerced, NOR type-bracketed. The spec documents no coercion rule of any kind for `>`, `>=`, `<`, `<=` or the three-argument between form, so string-versus-number bound behavior is undefined and falls to whichever of the eight language ports evaluates the rule. Failure mode: silent divergence — the same Recipe filters differently in two runtimes, with no error at either.
findings.evidence: Raw 67,354-byte HTML fetched and grepped, not just summarized. The entire relational section under "Numeric Operations" is four label fragments plus four all-numeric examples; every coercion sentence on the page is attached to an equality operator ("Tests equality, with type coercion" for ==, "Tests strict equality" for ===), never a relational one. The contrast strengthens the point: the page explicitly pins truthiness cross-interpreter ("JsonLogic has its own spec for truthy to ensure that rules will run consistently across interpreters... string \"0\" is truthy") and pointedly does not do so for comparison. Two honest qualifications from verification: the "Numeric Operations" heading is a weak categorical hint that these are meant for numbers, and "delegated to the eight implementations" is inference from documented silence — the page is simply mute. Bearing on querbeet: no external format will normalize "1000" vs 1000 for you; querbeet's own evaluator must define the coercion.

findings.claim: DECISION B, format survey — the other three rows CANNOT be filled from surviving evidence. The candidate claims for MongoDB (type-bracketed, silent empty result), Elasticsearch (coerces strings into the mapped type), OData 4.01 (typed by lexical form, quotes make it a String) and JsonLogic's ==/=== pair were all refuted 0-3 in verification and must not be cited. Treat the per-format comparison as one confirmed row and three open ones, not as a completed survey.
sources: verification record for this session (refuted set)
findings.evidence: Refuted at 0-3: the MongoDB BSON type-bracketing claim, the Elasticsearch coerce claim, the OData ABNF lexical-form claim, and both JsonLogic equality claims. A refuted claim means the cited source did not support it as stated — it does not establish the opposite, so these formats are unresolved rather than decided against. This matters because R5's decision does not depend on them: the LLM-authoring evidence plus JsonLogic's documented silence are jointly sufficient to close B, and re-running the survey would be confirmation work, not decision work.

findings.claim: DECISION B RECOMMENDATION — `value` is a JSON number in canonical machine form (dot decimal, no grouping separators) for numeric columns; a string only for genuinely textual comparisons. RUNNER-UP: `value` always a string in a canonical machine format, parsed by querbeet against the column's confirmed type and locale. Reject the third candidate (typed per condition) outright — it is the anyOf union under another name, and the Azure finding shows that shape is what produced the split.
findings.evidence: Three reasons the number wins over the plan's current lean. (1) It is the type the one working determinism mechanism targets — the vendor's own example treats 2 as correct and "2" as the incompatible type. (2) It is locale-free by construction, so it is MORE portable than a locale-parsed string, not less: FR-9 already makes locale a property of the column's source parsing, and putting locale into the comparison constant as well means a Consumer whose file is 1,234.56 inherits a bound written for 1.234,56. The research plan's premise that only the string form keeps a Recipe portable (line 619) does not survive this — a JSON number needs no locale to be read correctly anywhere. (3) A JSON number cannot be ambiguous the way the string "1.234" is; the string form re-imports the exact defect R1 and R3 measured (an anchored regex reading `.` as a decimal point) into the value field. The runner-up's one real advantage is precision — a JSON number is an IEEE-754 double in every JS parser, so cent-exact currency beyond 2^53 or long numeric IDs would need the string. That is the condition under which the runner-up should be promoted.

findings.claim: DECISION B ENFORCEMENT — whatever type is chosen is currently unenforced and undocumented to the model, and both gaps are in files that exist today. `proposed/columns.js` validates column names against the propagated schema; nothing anywhere inspects a value. `block-template.txt`'s only filter example is {"column":"Region","op":"equals","value":"Süd"} — a text comparison, which is why five authors guessed at the numeric case.
findings.evidence: Read directly. block-template.txt lines 74 and 128 both carry the same text-column filter example and no numeric one. columns.js (163 lines) is name validation only; load-recipe.mjs (42 lines) does JSON.parse and no value typing. Concrete shape of the fix, matching the number recommendation: accept a JSON number as-is; accept a string matching -?\d+(\.\d+)? by coercing it (this alone converts four of the five measured authorings, since "1000" is canonical); refuse anything with a grouping separator or comma decimal — "1.234,56", "1,000" — by name, in the same place and message style as an unknown column, so a Consumer never silently inherits a differently-filtering Recipe. Add one numeric filter example to block-template.txt on the same day, per the plan's own condition at line 626.

findings.claim: DECISION C — Tailwind v4 can be inlined next to @vue-flow/core's stylesheet with the reset removed entirely. `@import "tailwindcss"` decomposes into three layer imports; deleting only the `preflight.css` line yields utilities plus theme and no base reset, removing the collision the Vue Flow stylesheet would otherwise lose.
findings.evidence: Verified against both the rendered page and the raw MDX. Verbatim default structure: `@layer theme, base, components, utilities;` / `@import "tailwindcss/theme.css" layer(theme);` / `@import "tailwindcss/preflight.css" layer(base);` / `@import "tailwindcss/utilities.css" layer(utilities);` — and "To disable Preflight, simply omit its import while keeping everything else:" with the preflight line carrying a [!code --] deletion marker. Docs nav shows v4.3, so this is current and not a v4.0 artifact. Fits querbeet's build constraint directly: R2 established inlining everything into one file and nothing is fetchable at runtime from file://, and these are ordinary CSS imports resolved at build time by the Tailwind plugin, so vite-plugin-singlefile still sees one stylesheet.

findings.claim: DECISION C — Preflight-versus-third-party-stylesheet is an acknowledged collision in Tailwind's own docs, and disabling Preflight is offered as one of exactly two remedies (the other being per-element overrides in `@layer base`). Do not cite the refuted version of this claim, which wrongly asserted the override was the only prescribed fix.
findings.evidence: Page text: "This can cause some unexpected results when integrating certain third-party libraries, like [Google maps] for example", linking tailwindlabs/tailwindcss#484. The docs never name @vue-flow/core; applying the pattern to it is inference in the same collision direction (a reset clobbering styles a third-party stylesheet depends on), not documented fact. A stricter claim that the per-container override was the prescribed fix was refuted 0-3 precisely because disabling Preflight is presented as a general solution alongside it.

findings.claim: DECISION C RECOMMENDATION — Tailwind v4 with the three-line split import and no `preflight.css`, inlined at build. RUNNER-UP: hand-written CSS scoped to querbeet's own components. Pico.css is third and should be dropped: it is classless, so it styles bare elements globally — the same failure mode as Preflight, with no documented opt-out equivalent to omitting one import line.
findings.evidence: Sourced part: only Tailwind documents a first-class way to ship utilities without a global reset. Inference part, flagged as such: the Pico.css assessment reasons from its classless design and was not part of the verified evidence set — check it before it is written into a decision record. One caveat that must travel with the recommendation: the same Tailwind section warns that when importing the files individually, modifiers move onto their respective imports — source(…) and important onto utilities.css, theme(static)/theme(inline) onto theme.css, prefix(tw) onto both. If querbeet ever wants a tw- prefix to further insulate Vue Flow, it must be declared twice.

result.caveats: Three things bound this synthesis. First, the per-format survey is one confirmed row, not four: the MongoDB, Elasticsearch and OData claims were refuted 0-3 and are excluded, so the requested TYPED-BY-SYNTAX / COERCED / TYPE-BRACKETED assignment can only be given for JsonLogic, where the honest answer is a fourth category — undefined. Second, the strongest evidence for B is about what vendors document, not about measured model behavior: no source in this set says anything about locale-formatted columns or about authoring statistics, so the link from "unconstrained union" to "four-to-one split" is consistency, not causation, and the spike's n=5 remains the only measurement. Third, the one mechanism that provably fixes the type ambiguity — grammar-constrained sampling under strict: true — is an API-side feature querbeet structurally cannot use, since a Recipe is pasted in from an arbitrary external chat; every recommendation here therefore shifts enforcement to querbeet's own ingest validator, which is a design commitment rather than a research finding. The Pico.css judgement in the C recommendation is unsourced reasoning. WebSearch budget was exhausted during verification, so no independent third-party contradiction search backs the Anthropic and Tailwind rows.
openQuestions: Does the canonical-number rule generalize beyond numeric columns, or does {"op":"gt","value":"2025-12-31"} need a separate rule? Dates are the next comparison type an LLM will guess at, and FR-9 detects date locale per column too — a decision that covers only numbers leaves the same hole one column type over.

Does querbeet need precision beyond an IEEE-754 double — cent-exact currency above 2^53, or long numeric identifiers used as filter bounds? That is the single condition under which the string runner-up should be promoted over the number, and it should be answered before the format is frozen.

When a model emits a locale-formatted value like "1.234,56", should the loader refuse it by name or normalize it with a visible warning? FR-9's own stance is to report ambiguity rather than resolve it silently, which argues for refusal — but refusal punishes the Consumer for the Author's model, so the UX question is real.

Is the confirmed column type and locale recorded in the Recipe (plan line 639), and if so must the value type agree with it at load time — i.e. is a JSON number on a text-typed column an error? This decides whether value validation is a standalone check or a second consumer of the propagated schema columns.js already walks.

refuted.claim: MongoDB query comparison operators ($gt, $lt, etc.) are type-bracketed: a predicate only matches documents whose target field has the same BSON type as the query operand, so {"amount": {"$gt": "1000"}} (string bound) matches no numeric documents at all — silent empty result, not an error. This is the decisive answer for Gap B's MongoDB row: the comparison value is REQUIRED TO MATCH the field type, never coerced.
JsonLogic's `==` operator is defined to perform type coercion, so a string comparison value matches a numeric field value: the official docs give `{"==" : [1, "1"]}` as returning true.

JsonLogic ships a strict variant `===` under which the same operands do NOT match: `{"===" : [1, "1"]}` returns false, so whether a quoted "1000" matches a numeric 1000 depends entirely on which operator the rule author chose — the format itself does not type or coerce the comparison value.

With coercion enabled (the default for numeric fields), Elasticsearch COERCES a string comparison/ingest value into the field's mapped type — strings become numbers and floats are truncated to integers — so a string literal is accepted rather than type-mismatched.

In OData 4.01 the type of a comparison value is fixed by its lexical form, not coerced: numeric literals are unquoted by grammar (no SQUOTE in the decimalValue/int64Value productions) while a string literal is delimited by single quotes — so `amount gt '1000'` is grammatically a String literal, never a number.

Attaching a JSON schema to the request measurably increases prompt sensitivity and output variance: the authors report that removing the schema restriction produced higher average scores AND lower standard deviations across prompt variants. This is the paper's most direct evidence that schema shape — not just schema presence — changes how consistently a model emits a given field, which is the mechanism behind the observed four-to-one "1000" vs 1000 split.

The ORDER of keys in the supplied schema deterministically dictated generation order — 100% of GPT-3.5-Turbo JSON-mode responses emitted the 'answer' key before the 'reason' key when the schema listed them that way, collapsing chain-of-thought into direct answering. Schema authoring details are therefore load-bearing on model output, not cosmetic.

Tailwind's own documentation acknowledges that Preflight breaks third-party libraries that ship their own stylesheet, and cites a filed GitHub issue (tailwindlabs/tailwindcss#484, Google Maps) as the canonical example; the prescribed fix is a per-container override inside `@layer base`, not a general solution.
